content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with confidence 0.8. I used 55 of the 60 budget.

**Phase 1.** I trained 2 tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L2-S2-M2, so every rule appeared once. Here the factor-when-justified learner can't have any reusable parts yet, so it should behave like the holistic one. The results were too noisy to separate part-based from holistic. The same test returned 1 one time and 45 another. Costs roughly followed how similar a task was to the trained ones, but not cleanly. One task with two new rules and moderate similarity came out slower than a holistic learner predicts, which pointed slightly towards part-based.

**Phase 2.** This was the deciding test. I trained 7 more tasks so that each rule of the target L4-S1-M3 appeared in at least 3 trained tasks, which makes all three of its rules parts for either value of k. Its similarity to anything trained stayed low (0.375). I compared it with two controls that are more similar to the trained tasks but have fewer reusable parts:

| Task | Rule status | Max similarity | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| L4-S1-M3 (target) | all 3 rules seen 3+ times | 0.375 | 30.5 (n=10) |
| L4-S3-M1 | no new rules, but S3 and M1 seen only once | 0.5625 | 19.6 (n=8) |
| L3-S2-M4 | one new rule (L3) | 0.625 | 18.9 (n=8) |

- **Part-based** predicts the target is the fastest, or tied with L4-S3-M1.
- **Factor-when-justified** predicts the target is clearly the fastest.
- **Holistic** predicts the target is the slowest, because it is the least similar.

The target was the slowest, about 11 examples behind both controls. That gap is roughly twice its standard error. It also barely improved from before phase 2 (35.8 to 30.5) even though all its rules had become well practised. That fits a learner that only cares about overall similarity.

The 0.8 confidence reflects how noisy single tests are, and the phase 1 result that leaned towards part-based.
